gaps: Runaway integrations (residues where the ignition creates an escalating structural floor that makes decoupling ruinous, inverting the concept of a hard ceiling)
Asymmetric lock-ins (residues where the ignition permanently strips exit rights from one party while perfectly preserving them for the other)
Mechanism capture (residues where the necessary maintenance of the ignition structure, such as feeding a staged enemy or hiding a shared sin, eventually consumes the cooperation's actual yield)
accepted: Code in the vault: one party deposits the source code or a process manual with a third party to be released only on failure, as in software escrow; the carrier is the deposit, the first move is safe because the provider retains the asset while the user sees the safety net, and the residue is that the third party is now a permanent node in the loop; one side can strike this alone.

Crosscut saw: two parties must operate a single tool that neither can use alone, as a two-man saw or a two-key launch system; the carrier is the physical asset, the first move is safe because neither party can extract value alone, and the residue is that the work stops the moment one party lets go; both hands must strike at once.

Symmetrical cup: two parties consume the same thing from the same source at the same time, as drinking from one bottle or eating from one dish; the carrier is the shared physical exposure, the first move is safe because the risk of harm is perfectly symmetrical, and the residue is that trust remains limited to non-aggression; both hands must strike at once.

residue.item: Unpaid pilot: one party performs a sample of work to the other’s specific requirement for no fee, as a translator does a test page or a developer solves a dummy bug; the carrier is the sunk labor, the first move is safe because the cost is a controlled loss for the performer, and the residue is that the performer has signaled a lower bound on their price, [Author's inference: which the buyer then adopts as the baseline]; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Contains a bracketed '[Author's inference...]' which breaks the grain; the prompt indicates that authorial inferences are marked analytically within the boundary claims or inline text organically, not with literal meta-brackets.

residue.item: Open kitchen: one party allows the other to observe the labor process without revealing the final product, as a chef works behind glass or a coder streams a build; the carrier is the visibility of the method, the first move is safe because watching costs the performer nothing, and the residue is that the "how" is now public property, [Author's inference: so the performer can no longer price the secret, only the execution]; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Breaks the text's grain by explicitly inserting an unnatural '[Author's inference...]' bracket.

residue.item: Burned bridge: one party publicly destroys their own alternative before the deal is done, as a partner closes their own shop to join a stranger or a worker quits a job to take a risk; the carrier is the destroyed option, the first move is safe because it proves commitment by force, and the residue is that the mover has no retreat, [Author's inference: making them vulnerable to a later squeeze]; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Breaks the text's grain with the literal bracketed tag '[Author's inference...]'.

residue.item: Rented brand: a high-value firm allows a stranger to use its trademark for a limited venture, as a franchisor or a joint-venture partner; the carrier is the trademark license, the first move is safe because the owner will not wreck their brand for a petty win, and the residue is that the brand dictates the terms of growth, [Author's inference: and the small partner never outgrows the shadow]; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Breaks the text's grain with the literal bracketed tag '[Author's inference...]'.

residue.item: Tied handset: one party gives away a base unit that requires the other’s specific part to function, as a free printer needing specific ink or a handset on one network; the carrier is the incomplete tool, the first move is safe because the giver profits only on the back end, and the residue is an ecosystem lock-in where the receiver is captured by the giver’s supply chain; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Ambiguous phrasing. It states the base unit 'requires the other's specific part to function' but the example 'free printer needing specific ink' implies the receiver must buy the giver's part, contradicting 'the other's'.

residue.item: Bond on deposit: one party places a sum with a third party that the counterpart can claim on a simple condition, as a performance bond or a security deposit; the carrier is the escrowed cash, the first move is safe because the holder has immediate recourse, and the residue is that the cooperation is bounded by the bond’s value; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: Explicitly excluded by the existing text under 'Hostage before the ask', which notes: 'not source escrow or a bond, where a third party holds the thing...'. Keeping it would contradict the list's established boundaries.

residue.item: Public bounty: one party offers a reward to anyone who can provide a specific result, as a bug bounty or a reward for a lost item; the carrier is the public offer, the first move is safe for the respondent because the reward is public and for the offeror because they only pay for results, and the residue is that the winner is already looking for the next bounty; one side can strike this alone.
residue.why: A public bounty operates on the exact same mechanism as 'Rule against myself'—binding oneself publicly to terms before a stranger arrives. It is not distinct.

residue.item: Multi-sig key: two parties each hold a part of a cryptographic or physical key required to move an asset; the carrier is the split protocol, the first move is safe because the first party to provide their half risks nothing without the second, and the residue is a mutual veto that can freeze the asset in a stalemate; both hands must strike at once.
residue.why: Functionally redundant with the escrow mechanisms ('Code in the vault') and 'Crosscut saw'; providing half a key safely relies on protocol architecture, which overlaps too heavily with existing technical/third-party locks.

residue.item: Commingled silo: two parties mix their fungible goods for storage or transport to save costs, as grain in a silo or oil in a pipe; the carrier is the indistinguishable bulk, the first move is safe because the volume buffers individual loss, and the residue is shared liability for any shrink; both hands must strike at once.
residue.why: Mixing goods in a silo does not intrinsically make the first move safe against a bad actor; it relies entirely on the silo operator being a trusted third-party enforcer.

residue.item: Joint petition: two parties add their names to a single demand or letter to a third party; the carrier is the shared document, the first move is safe because the reputational hit is shared equally, and the residue is a permanent public alignment in the eyes of the target; both hands must strike at once.
residue.why: Redundant with 'Sin in common' (transgression both commit) combined with 'Summoned witness' or 'Enemy at both doors'. Not mechanically distinct.

residue.item: Shared charter: two parties are placed in a vehicle with a fixed destination, as strangers in a long-haul sleeper or firms sharing a freight charter; the carrier is the shared transit, the first move is safe because the destination is shared and the cost of stopping is high for both, and the residue is that the cooperation ends at the terminal; a third with a stake can strike this.
residue.why: Conceptually identical to 'Same cell' (an imposed future in a shared space where cooperation is an artifact of the cage).

residue.item: Common tap: two parties draw from a resource that neither owns but both require, as an aquifer or a public grazing land; the carrier is the geography of the resource, the first move is safe because each must preserve the resource to use it themselves, and the residue is a truce against depletion; nobody can strike this.
residue.why: Describes a Tragedy of the Commons. The claim that 'each must preserve the resource to use it themselves' is empirically false in unmanaged commons, making it a failed mechanism for cooperation.

residue.item: Fit that requires the source: one party installs hardware that only the other can supply or service, as a lab buys a sequencer that only takes the stranger’s proprietary reagents or a factory installs a furnace that only fits one firm’s crucibles; the carrier is a hardware specification pinned in the order, the first move is safe because the machine is sold at a discount or leased, and the residue is a lock-in where the owner cannot switch suppliers without scrapping the capital; struck by the buyer alone.
residue.why: Relies fundamentally on external legal contracts to make the unilateral sunk cost survivable for the buyer. Without a court, the supplier could infinitely extort the locked-in buyer, violating the core constraint.

residue.item: Logic as a graft: one party builds its own software to call a stranger’s specific functions, as a startup builds its app on a proprietary API or a bank routes its core ledger through a niche clearinghouse’s schema; the carrier is the written API documentation, the first move is safe because the integration is free and speeds the build, and the residue is that the codebase is now a graft that cannot be pruned without a total rewrite; struck by the developer alone.
residue.why: Like candidate 15, this relies on a stable external legal/market environment. The first move is not intrinsically safe from platform rug-pulling.

residue.item: Tab that never closes: two parties agree to track future favors in a rolling tally rather than settling each deal, as two off-book crews trade shifts or two neighbors trade tractor hours; the carrier is a written rolling balance, the first move is safe because the first favor is small, and the residue is that the parties can never zero the account without losing the "credit" they’ve built, making the relationship a perpetual motion machine where the only way to get paid is to keep playing; struck by both hands at once.
residue.why: Describes 'recursive gift exchange, which is the running loop'. The boundary claim explicitly excludes 'what keeps cooperation running once lit' as being outside the map.

residue.item: Paperwork as a cage: one party trains its staff in the other’s internal jargon and idiosyncratic manifests to make the first deal possible, as a freight forwarder adopts a specific port’s customs workflow or a subcontractor learns a prime’s proprietary safety protocol; the carrier is the written manual or manifest template, the first move is safe because it costs only training time, and the residue is a sunk cost of human capital that makes any other partner look expensive by comparison; struck by the learner alone.
residue.why: Mechanically identical to 'First cut' (destroying an outside option/sinking specific capital to prove commitment to one counterpart).

residue.item: Sunk substrate: one party provides the foundational layer upon which the other builds its operation, as a landlord provides the specialized ventilation and grease traps for a restaurant or a cloud provider gives free credits to a new dev; the carrier is a site-specific lease addendum or service agreement, the first move is safe because it is a windfall, and the residue is that the receiver’s business is now a tenant of the giver’s systems, where the cost of moving out is higher than the value of the business; struck by the giver alone.
residue.why: A landlord providing a foundation is only safe for the tenant because of a lease agreement backed by courts. Without enforcement, the tenant's business could be seized.

residue.item: Single index for two houses: two parties adopt a shared taxonomy or indexing system for their separate goods so they can be traded at volume, as two libraries adopt one unique shelf-code or two parts-bins use one numbering system; the carrier is the shared schema document, the first move is safe because it organizes the house, and the residue is that neither can change their internal logic without breaking the link to the other, creating a structural floor that grows with every new item added; struck by nobody.
residue.why: Philosophically contradictory: if 'two parties adopt' the system, then the ignition is struck by both parties, contradicting the claim that it is 'struck by nobody'.

residue.item: Fixtures for the next man: one party installs permanent improvements on another's ground, as a restaurateur tiles a landlord's kitchen or a shopkeeper plumbs a leased bay; the carrier is the immobility of the investment, the first move is safe for the landlord because the value stays even if the tenant fails, one side alone can strike it by performing the build-out, and the residue is that the tenant's exit cost is the whole investment while the landlord remains free to re-rent the upgrade to anyone.
residue.why: Just like 15 and 19, making permanent improvements on another's land requires a court-backed lease to be safe for the tenant, violating the 'no enforcer required' constraint.

residue.item: Plug for one socket: one party builds its tool to fit only the other's proprietary standard, as a software dev writes for one OS or a component maker shapes a part for one engine; the carrier is technical specificity, the first move is safe for the socket-owner because they gain a tool without changing their system, one side alone can strike it by choosing the standard, and the residue is that the builder is captive to the socket-owner's updates while the owner can swap builders without changing the socket.
residue.why: Unilateral technical asset specificity. The first move is not intrinsically safe for the builder (the vulnerable party) without a legal framework preventing the platform from stealing the yield.

residue.item: Sign on the roof: one party adopts the other's brand identity to get the first customer, as a franchisee builds a store to one spec or a dealer takes an exclusive territory; the carrier is the brand’s public trust, the first move is safe for the brand because the store is built to its spec and costs it nothing, one side alone can strike it by accepting the license, and the residue is that the dealer cannot pivot to new goods while the brand can saturate the map or go direct.
residue.why: The franchisee takes a massive naked risk that is entirely unsafe without franchise law enforcement standing behind the paper.

residue.item: Archive in your vault: one party moves its history into the other's proprietary format or silo, as a firm migrates its records to a vendor’s cloud or a user commits their archive to one platform; the carrier is the cost of extraction, the first move is safe for the host because the volume adds to their scale and requires no trust, one side alone can strike it by clicking import, and the residue is an exit tax where the owner must pay to leave while the host can raise prices without fearing flight.
residue.why: Archiving in a vendor's silo is unsafe for the user without data-protection contracts. The mechanism itself doesn't ensure cooperation.

residue.item: Training for the fleet: one party trains its staff specifically to operate the other's idiosyncratic equipment, as a pilot learns a specific airframe or a mechanic learns a single brand’s diagnostic tool; the carrier is non-transferable skill, the first move is safe for the operator because the staff becomes ready to work on their terms, one side alone can strike it by starting the class, and the residue is that the staff's value is zero to any rival while the operator can replace them with any other certified hand.
residue.why: Human capital lock-in. Same structural flaw as other asset-specificity examples: the bare payoffs leave the mover completely exposed without a contract.

residue.item: Pipeline in the trench: one party runs its infrastructure through the other's right-of-way, as a telco lays fiber in a rail bed or a utility runs a pipe through a neighbor’s lot; the carrier is a physical path, the first move is safe for the landowner because the line adds no liability to the ground and pays a fee, one side alone can strike it by laying the line, and the residue is that the builder's entire network is broken if the path is pulled while the landowner can revoke the path and keep their lot intact.
residue.why: Laying a pipeline in another's trench without a legally binding easement is suicide, not a safe first move.

residue.item: Shared leash: two parties use a third-party’s proprietary platform to transact where no open channel exists, as two vendors coordinate through a delivery app’s hidden chat or two traders use a dark pool; the carrier is a private infrastructure that monitors the pair, the first move is safe because the platform logs every deviation and punishes it with exclusion, and the residue is that the platform captures the data and eventually the margin, so the partners become sub-contractors to their own ignition; a third with a stake can strike it.
residue.why: A proprietary platform that logs deviations and punishes with exclusion is a literal enforcer contract, explicitly violating the boundary claims.

residue.item: Feeding the shadow: two parties hire a fixer to facilitate a move that bypasses a rule, as two developers pay a consultant to navigate a zoning board or two firms hire a lobbyist to hold their shared slush fund; the carrier is a third party whose silence is the only bond, the first move is safe because the fixer’s business relies on being a reliable vault, and the residue is that the fixer’s fee grows to match the cooperation’s yield until the partners are working for the shadow; both hands at once can strike it.
residue.why: Hiring a fixer requires the parties to already coordinate and trust the third party, making it a secondary action rather than a bare first ignition between strangers.

residue.item: Manufactured wall: one party sabotages its own asset to force a joint repair with a stranger who holds the only tool, as a ship captain fouls a line to justify a tow from a rival or a tech lead breaks a legacy module to force a contract with the only dev who knows it; the carrier is a simulated wall neither can lift, the first move is safe because the repair is genuinely necessary once the break is made, and the residue is that the stager must keep breaking things to maintain the emergency that justifies the partnership, turning the yield into a repair fund; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: Sabotaging one's own asset to force a stranger to repair it simply allows the stranger to charge a monopoly price (extortion); it does not ignite a mutual cooperation forbidden by bare payoffs.

residue.item: Umbrella rent: two parties operate under a single franchise or license owned by a third to avoid competing on terms, as two independent pharmacies join one buying group or two drivers share one medallion; the carrier is a shared regulatory umbrella, the first move is safe because the licensor dictates the conduct and takes the risk of the word, and the residue is that the licensor eventually raises the rent to absorb the cooperation's efficiency, leaving the partners as mere operators of the ignition; a third with a stake can strike it.
residue.why: A shared regulatory umbrella is essentially a managed cartel orchestrated by a third-party licensor, relying entirely on the licensor's legal authority.

residue.item: Shared take: two parties pay a single official to overlook a shared transgression, ensuring neither can report the other without being reported by the taker, as two contractors pay one inspector or two ships pay one harbor master; the carrier is the corrupt record held by the official, the first move is safe because the official’s own career is the hostage, and the residue is that the official’s tax scales with the cooperation's success until the parties are essentially employees of the witness; a third with a stake can strike it.
residue.why: Paying an official is simply bribing a tollbooth. The mutual deterrence created is mechanically identical to 'Sin in common' mixed with a third-party broker.

residue.item: Prestige debt: one party gifts a high-maintenance status asset that the other must help maintain to keep its own reputation, as a developer builds a public park that the city must co-fund or a donor gives a museum a collection that requires a new wing; the carrier is a white elephant that confers shared status, the first move is safe because the public optics of failure are too high for either to walk away, and the residue is that the upkeep of the symbol eventually outpaces its utility, leaving the parties bound to a monument that eats their budget; one side alone can strike it.
residue.why: A white elephant gift maintained only because of the 'public optics of failure' is simply a variant of the 'Summoned witness' mechanism applied as a trap.

stance: Work in this stance: control. Ask of the list, what must be pinned down in writing?

gaps: Writing to legally sever the future (e.g., the explicit liability waiver or 'as-is' clause, where the text's only function is to destroy the shadow of the future to make a spot move safe)
Writing as a compliant decoy (where a text pins down a fictional clean deal strictly to satisfy a regulator's gaze, sheltering the real unwritten cooperation beneath it)
Writing as the self-executing payload (e.g., the dead-man's switch or escrowed cryptographic key, where the text itself is the hostage that drops if the counterpart defaults)
accepted: Socket before the plug: one party provides a technical interface or mounting standard the other must build to, as a software platform exposes an API for a stranger’s plugin or a truck manufacturer releases its chassis specs; the carrier is a technical geometry, the first move is safe because the host controls the environment and the guest bears the integration cost, and the residue is path dependency, where the guest is a permanent tenant of the host’s logic and the host cannot pivot without breaking the guest; one side strikes it alone.

Salt in the data: one party provides information containing minor, harmless errors that act as tracers, as a mapmaker includes trap streets or a mailing list owner includes seed addresses; the carrier is an intentional error, the first move is safe because the errors are harmless to a legitimate user and only identify a thief, and the residue is that the receiver knows the data is a trap and the giver knows the receiver is a potential thief, so the data never flows clean; one side strikes it alone.

Locked choice: the carrier is a hashed commitment to a value or a bid that cannot be changed once the counterpart sees the hash, as a contractor hashes a bid or a lab locks its trial design; the first move is safe because the choice is hidden until the reveal and the ignition is the proof that the choice was made before the other's was known; it can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is that the parties are bound to their first instincts and the winner’s regret is locked in by the math of the opening.

Fragmented key: the carrier is a secret or a fund split into parts such that neither party can use it alone but either can prevent the other, as a treasurer and a chair split a vault's combination or two firms share a multi-sig wallet; the first move is safe because the stake is immobilized and neither side can abscond; it can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is a permanent mutual veto, where the cooperation ends in a frozen asset the moment one party stops speaking.

residue.item: Half-map at the merge: two parties each hold a piece of information that is worthless alone but valuable together, as two firms share parts of a cryptographic key to unlock a data room or two treasure hunters each hold half a chart; the carrier is information symmetry, the first move is safe because neither side can act on its own part, and the residue is that the value is only in the sum, so neither party learns how the other treats a surplus they could take alone; both hands strike it at once.
residue.why: Violates the boundary condition that no item is invented-world (treasure hunters holding half a map is a fictional trope).

residue.item: Empty backhaul: a carrier with a sunk cost for a returning vehicle offers the capacity to a stranger at a marginal rate, as a trucking firm with an empty leg or a passenger ship with a deadhead cabin; the carrier is the waste of a primary business, the first move is safe because any revenue is pure margin and the trip is happening anyway, and the residue is subordinate status, where the guest only moves when the host is already going and the cooperation never dictates the schedule; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: An empty backhaul is simply pricing a sunk cost at marginal rate; the bare payoffs actively encourage this, so it does not overcome a cooperation hurdle where bare payoffs would forbid the move.

residue.item: Seed in the furrow: one party contributes a non-retrievable input to the other’s asset, as a developer submits a patch to a stranger's repository or a tenant applies fertilizer to a landlord’s field; the carrier is an irreversible improvement, the first move is safe because the input is small compared to the total yield and the provider doesn't lose the original knowledge, and the residue is that the provider becomes a supplicant for the harvest and cannot move the seed to a different field; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Not sufficiently distinct from 'Lot you can lose'. The safety mechanism relies entirely on the input being a small, affordable loss, which is the exact mechanism of the divisible lot.

residue.item: Key to the outer gate: one party grants access to a perimeter while keeping the core secured, as a homeowner gives a contractor the key to the mudroom but not the house or a server admin grants a user access to a staging environment; the carrier is partitioned access, the first move is safe because the main assets are still behind a second lock, and the residue is that trust is physically bounded and the inner remains a secret even if the work is perfect; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Conceptually overlaps heavily with 'Lot you can lose' by just capping the downside, acting as standard risk mitigation rather than a distinct ignition of trust.

residue.item: Bounty for the bug: one party binds itself to pay whoever finds a specific flaw, as a software firm offers a bug bounty or a warehouse offers a reward for a lost pallet; the carrier is a standing open offer, the first move is safe because the reward is priced lower than the value of the fix and the find is verified before payment, and the residue is that the relationship is purely mercenary and the partner only speaks when there is a hole to be filled; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: A standing open offer is structurally identical to 'Rule against myself' (binding oneself publicly to terms before a stranger arrives).

residue.item: Bridge to the property line: one party builds infrastructure that terminates at the other’s boundary, as a developer builds a road to the edge of a neighbor’s parcel or a cable company runs fiber to a building’s basement; the carrier is a fixed physical path, the first move is safe because the builder owns the asset on their own land and only the connection is at risk, and the residue is that the connection point is a permanent constraint on the layout of all future growth; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Building infrastructure on one's own land doesn't inherently overcome a trust deficit or ignite cooperation; it is just a sunk cost or standard physical preparation.

residue.item: Shadow in the kitchen: one party allows the other to observe its process without participating, as a restaurant lets an apprentice watch the line or a firm lets a prospective partner shadow a project; the carrier is unpaid observation, the first move is safe because the observer does not touch the tools or the product, and the residue is that the observer has seen the backstage mess and can never again be impressed by the brand’s public mask; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Unpaid observation carries no real risk or potential payoff structure that would ordinarily forbid the interaction.

residue.item: Sample from the middle: one party allows the other to take a core-cut or a random slice of a bulk good, as a grain buyer probes a hopper or a fabric buyer cuts a swatch from the center of a bolt; the carrier is a representative probe of a mass, the first move is safe because the cost is one piece of a large lot, and the residue is that the probe only proves the past batch and not the partner’s future intent, so the parties are locked in constant re-sampling; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: A sample from the middle is just a quality-inspection variant of 'Lot you can lose'. The mechanism of safety (the cost is one small piece of a large lot) is identical to divisibility.

residue.item: Trial by fire: one party stages a minor crisis to observe how the other responds under pressure, as a manager gives a new hire a dead lead to test persistence or a security firm triggers a false alarm to watch the guard’s reaction; the carrier is a manufactured emergency, the first move is safe because the stager controls the safety valve, and the residue is that the responder's competence is proven but their resentment is a permanent risk if the stage is ever discovered; the claim that a staged circumstance inherits the probe's residue is the author's analytical inference; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Too similar to 'Twenty in the till' (a staged test of the counterpart). Furthermore, the text clumsily pastes the author's meta-commentary directly into the residue, violating the grain.

residue.item: Tap on the main: two parties connect to a shared utility that neither owns or controls, as two neighbors tap the same public water main or two firms use the same public cloud region; the carrier is a shared resource header, the first move is safe because the utility provider manages the flow and neither party can shut the other off, and the residue is that usage is zero-sum and the cooperation is limited to the utility’s capacity; nobody strikes it.
residue.why: Violates the boundary condition by relying on a third-party enforcer (the utility provider) to manage the flow and enforce safety.

residue.item: Pilot in the wheelhouse: a third party with specific local knowledge takes control of one party’s asset to move it through a dangerous passage, as a harbor pilot steers a ship or a fixer handles a stranger's local negotiation; the carrier is licensed expertise, the first move is safe because the pilot is bonded and the owner stays on board, and the residue is that the owner admits they cannot navigate the channel alone and remains dependent on the pilot's guild; a third with a stake strikes it.
residue.why: Relies on a licensed/bonded enforcer (the pilot's guild) to make the move safe, violating the 'neither party's word/no enforcer' condition.

residue.item: Tear sheet for the spend: one party provides proof of money already spent on the other's behalf before any payment is made, as an ad agency shows the tear sheets of a campaign it ran for a client's product or a subcontractor buys the non-returnable materials for a job; the carrier is a record of sunk cost, the first move is safe because the money is already gone and the payer has skin in the game, and the residue is that the payer has bought a moral seat at the table and the receiver feels the weight of a debt they didn't price; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: A record of sunk cost operates on the same mechanism as 'First cut' (destroying an outside option/spending money to prove commitment).

residue.item: Surveyor’s mark: a third party validates the state of a good before it moves, as a marine surveyor inspects a hull or a white-hat hacker audits a codebase before a merger; the carrier is a third-party certificate, the first move is safe because the deal only ignites if the mark is clear, and the residue is that the parties trust the inspector's checklist rather than each other's standards, so the cooperation is only as deep as the audit; a third with a stake strikes it.
residue.why: Relies on a third-party auditor/certificate, violating the condition that the first move rests on neither stranger's word and without an external enforcer.

residue.item: As-is on the floor: the carrier is the explicit disclaimer of warranty in a spot sale, the first move is safe for the seller because the liability for a lemon ends at the exchange, making the stranger’s cash as good as a friend’s, and can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is that the buyer has no channel for grievance and the seller no reason to care if the machine breaks in the driveway, so the cooperation ends at the handover.
residue.why: Explicit legal clauses like an 'as-is' disclaimer are excluded because the contract itself is what makes the move safe.

residue.item: Permission to bleed: the carrier is the liability waiver signed before entering a dangerous site or starting a risky service, the first move is safe for the host because the stranger’s injury cannot become the host’s ruin, and can be struck by one side alone; the residue is that safety becomes the visitor's private cost, so the host has no incentive to improve the ground and the cooperation is bounded by the stranger’s own caution.
residue.why: A liability waiver relies entirely on the legal contract to shield the host, violating the boundary condition.

residue.item: Nothing but the paper: the carrier is the merger clause stating the document is the complete and final agreement, the first move is safe because it destroys the legal weight of every promise or vibe from the negotiation, and can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is that the parties are deaf to each other’s intent and the cooperation is brittle, as any adjustment to the reality of the work is a breach unless the paper is rewritten.
residue.why: A merger clause is purely a contractual shield, violating the condition that the list excludes cases where the contract itself is what makes the move safe.

residue.item: Skin only in the game: the carrier is the non-recourse clause limiting the lender's recovery to the collateral alone, the first move is safe for the borrower because their other assets are shielded from the stranger’s claim, and can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is that the lender has no interest in the borrower’s survival, only in the asset’s value, so the partnership is a bet on a thing and not a trust in a person.
residue.why: A non-recourse clause relies entirely on court enforcement of the contract, violating the boundary claim.

residue.item: Death at the bell: the carrier is the sunset clause that terminates a right or license on a fixed date without notice or cause, the first move is safe for the grantor because the stranger’s presence is guaranteed to be temporary, and can be struck by both hands at once; the residue is that the grantee cannot invest for the long term, so the cooperation is extractive and the parties never build the shared infrastructure that a permanent deal would fund.
residue.why: A sunset clause is an explicit contractual term that relies on a court/enforcer to be meaningful, which is excluded.

residue.item: The clean release: the carrier is the general release of all known and unknown claims, the first move is safe because the payer can resolve a sudden incident or clear a title without investigating the whole history of the right, and can be struck by one side alone; the residue is that the giver is permanently severed from the asset or the dispute even if they later find they were the rightful owner, so the exit is a clean break that forbids any return.
residue.why: A general release is a legal document enforced by a court, excluded by the boundary rules.

residue.item: Consultant’s ghost: one party pays for a report that satisfies a compliance officer to mask a bribe or a finder’s fee, as a firm hires a politician’s sibling for 'market research'; the carrier is a generic professional services invoice, the first move is safe because the fee is priced as a routine business expense, both hands at once strike it by signing the sham engagement, and the residue is that the payer can never demand real work and the receiver is permanently compromised by the paper trail of fraud.
residue.why: A sham invoice to hide a bribe is just a specific instance of 'Sin in common' (a transgression both commit).

residue.item: Professional-use lease: a landlord and a tenant sign for a permitted use in a space the parties know is for a forbidden one, as a landlord and tenant sign for an 'office' used as a speakeasy; the carrier is a standard-form agreement that mirrors the city’s zoning map, the first move is safe because the inspector sees a clean file and the rent is paid, both hands at once strike it by executing the decoy, and the residue is that the tenant cannot sue for repairs and the landlord can evict for a 'lease violation' the moment a better offer arrives.
residue.why: A decoy lease is another direct instance of 'Sin in common'.

residue.item: Dollar-bill title: the parties record the sale of a valuable asset for a token sum to bypass transfer taxes or disclosure, as a taxi medallion is transferred for ten dollars while the cash moves in a bag; the carrier is a bill of sale for a nominal amount, the first move is safe because the tax authority accepts the completed form and the real price is handled in cash, both hands at once strike it by filing the transfer, and the residue is that the buyer has no claim for a refund and the seller cannot prove the debt if the cash is short.
residue.why: A false bill of sale to bypass taxes is structurally identical to 'Sin in common'.

residue.item: Clerical-minimum roll: an employer and a worker sign a contract for the statutory minimum while the worker returns a portion in cash, as a restaurant worker signs for the legal minimum and returns a portion to the till; the carrier is a payroll ledger that satisfies the labor board, the first move is safe because the paper satisfies the inspector and the employer holds the physical cash, one side alone strikes it by signing the receipt, and the residue is that the worker loses all standing for underpayment and the employer lives under the threat of a whistleblower’s report.
residue.why: A fake payroll ledger is identical in mechanism to 'Sin in common'.

residue.item: Sole-source spec: a buyer writes a public tender with technical requirements that only one specific vendor’s machine can meet, as a city agency tender for trucks specifies a wheelbase only one maker builds; the carrier is a procurement document that appears competitive but is a lock, the first move is safe because the buyer avoids the delay of a bid while appearing to follow the rule, one side alone strikes it by publishing the criteria, and the residue is that the vendor can hold the buyer up on all subsequent parts and the buyer cannot switch without admitting the original spec was rigged.
residue.why: A rigged sole-source spec operates as a form of 'Sin in common' between the buyer and vendor to bypass procurement rules.

residue.item: Repair-only manifest: a shipper labels a cargo of forbidden goods as 'items for repair and return' to bypass an export ban or tariff, as a shipper labels a cargo of parts to bypass a duty; the carrier is a customs declaration for a non-sale, the first move is safe because no duty is paid and the cargo moves under a temporary bond, one side alone strikes it by declaring the transit, and the residue is that the goods must eventually be 'returned' on paper to close the bond, so the parties are chained to a second fiction.
residue.why: A false customs manifest to bypass tariffs is exactly 'Sin in common'.

residue.item: Triggered secret: the carrier is an encrypted payload held by a server scheduled to publish at a deadline unless the sender checks in, as a whistleblower’s cache or an operative's insurance; the first move is safe because the secret remains hidden while the timer runs, giving the counterpart a window to meet demands; it can be struck by one side alone; the residue is that the secret’s existence is now a known quantity, so the relationship is a peace kept by a gun that never unloads.
residue.why: An encrypted dead man's switch is a mechanism of extortion or mutually assured destruction, not a first cooperative move.

residue.item: Source escrow: the carrier is a cryptographic key or source code held by a neutral agent that releases only upon a defined failure, as a software licensee vaults the source against a developer's bankruptcy; the first move is safe because the user gets the tool today while the developer keeps the IP until the disaster; it can be struck by a third with a stake; the residue is that the user can never audit the logic while the developer lives and the developer can never fully pivot the product without the vault’s shadow.
residue.why: Explicitly relies on a contract and a neutral agent (an enforcer) to make the move safe. Additionally, attributing 'a third with a stake' to a neutral escrow agent contradicts the meaning of a stakeholder.

residue.item: Resignation in the drawer: the carrier is a signed, undated letter of withdrawal or a blank stock transfer handed to a partner or a lender; the first move is safe because the paper sits idle while the signer performs and the holder gains nothing by a premature strike that collapses the venture; it can be struck by one side alone; the residue is that the signer remains a permanent guest in their own house and the cooperation is a series of stays of execution.
residue.why: A resignation letter handed to a partner is a literal hostage, duplicating 'Hostage before the ask'.

residue.item: Time-locked refund: the carrier is a transaction pre-written to return a stake to the sender after a fixed duration, held in the same logic as the payment; the first move is safe because the sender knows the writing will claw back the value if the counterpart never moves; it can be struck by nobody; the residue is that the cooperation has a hard expiration and any delay by the counterpart becomes a theft of the sender's time.
residue.why: Incorrectly categorizes who can strike it as 'nobody' (since the sender must explicitly initiate it). Additionally, relying purely on programmatic logic mirrors a smart contract, which operates as a flawless enforcer.

stance: Work in this stance: control. Ask of the list, what must be pinned down in writing?

gaps: Kinetic emergencies (acute environmental shocks, like a sudden storm or fire, that collapse the timeline for trust and force immediate, unplanned operational parity, distinct from the static liability of a wall)
Hostile entanglements (one party intentionally forces a cooperative negotiation by seizing a minor asset or creating a reversible nuisance, igniting exchange through manufactured duress)
Blind pooling (mechanisms where counterparts are structurally anonymized and aggregated, meaning the first move is made with a protocol or a clearinghouse rather than an identifiable stranger)
accepted: Overflow on the desk: one party passes a lead it cannot serve to a stranger, as a booked-up plumber sends a homeowner to a rival; the carrier is the excess lead, the first move is safe because the lead was already a loss and the receiver gets a free trial, and the residue is a hierarchy where the receiver looks to the giver for crumbs and the giver has set the receiver's ceiling; one side strikes it alone.

Table at the show: one party pays the entry fee for a shared space both need, as a firm pays the booth fee for a joint exhibition; the carrier is a sunk access cost, the first move is safe because the payer needed access anyway and the partner makes the booth look busy, and the residue is that the payer owns the door and the partner is a guest; one side strikes it alone.

residue.item: Offcut in the bin: one party leaves byproduct where the other can take it without asking, as a cabinetmaker leaves hardwood scraps for a carver or a developer leaves an open API; the carrier is a waste stream, the first move is safe because the cost is sunk and the use is free, and the residue is a parasite's dependency, as the receiver's model is now indexed to the giver's trash; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Not a cooperative move that bare payoffs forbid; taking free byproduct is exactly what bare payoffs suggest, lacking mutual ignition.

residue.item: Cipher without the key: one party delivers a valuable but encrypted asset and holds the key, as a data scientist sends a model's output or a seeker sends a map's half; the carrier is a fragmented asset, the first move is safe because the fragment is useless alone, and the residue is that the relationship is a ransom, where the next move is always the only way to unlock the first; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Providing an encrypted asset without a key is a ransom or hold-up dynamic, not a cooperative first move.

residue.item: Key in the cab: one party leaves specialized tools at the other’s site to be used between shifts, as a contractor leaves the excavator on the lot or a chef leaves a knife roll; the carrier is a functional tool, the first move is safe because the owner can reclaim the tool and the holder advances the shared work, and the residue is that the work becomes shaped by the tool's specific edge; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Duplicate mechanism and example of 'Hostage before the ask' (leaving an excavator on the lot to show commitment).

residue.item: Typo in the terms: one party leaves an "accidental" benefit in a draft to see if the other points it out, as a lawyer includes a broad indemnity or a vendor under-quotes a line; the carrier is a beneficial error, the first move is safe because the giver can claim a mistake and the receiver's silence is a reading, and the residue is a shared secret of the corrected baseline that can never be acknowledged; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Duplicate mechanism of 'Twenty in the till' (staging a beneficial error/windfall to test the counterpart).

residue.item: Blind sheet from the agent: a third party shows one's work-product to the other without names, as a headhunter shows a masked resume; the carrier is de-identified work, the first move is safe because no names are at risk until the fit is proven, and the residue is that the first move was a curated highlight, making the later reality of the full person feel like a bait-and-switch; a third with a stake strikes it.
residue.why: Parties do not make a move with each other; relies entirely on the third-party agent, heavily overlapping 'Broker of both names'.

residue.item: Multisig in the vault: both parties lock an asset in a container neither can open alone, as two developers on a joint wallet; the carrier is a distributed authorization, the first move is safe because the asset is frozen until both agree, and the residue is the risk of a mutual bonfire where a deadlock destroys the value for both; both hands strike it at once.
residue.why: Relies entirely on cryptographic contract enforcement (smart contract vault), violating the condition that the move does not rely on a contract.

residue.item: Consignment on the shelf: the seller places goods on the buyer's floor and is paid only when they sell, as a new brand in a boutique; the carrier is the floor space, the first move is safe for the buyer because there is no capital risk and for the seller because they keep the title, and the residue is that the buyer never learns to value the brand enough to buy it upfront; both hands strike it at once.
residue.why: Relies fundamentally on the legal enforcement of title and property rights (a court standing behind the paper), violating the premise.

residue.item: Mark on the door: one party allows the other to use its trademark to signal quality, as a "Powered by" logo or a franchise sign; the carrier is a tethered reputation, the first move is safe for the receiver because the giver's name is the shield, and the residue is that the giver has a permanent veto over the receiver's standards, as any slip stains the mark; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Trademark licensing is inherently a legal contract framework, not an unwritten, uncoerced first move.

residue.item: Manual in the box: one party hands over its internal processes before the work begins, as a franchisor shares the manual or a coder shares internal docs; the carrier is a proprietary method, the first move is safe because the method is inert without the giver's support, and the residue is a mental cage where the receiver can no longer imagine doing the work any other way; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Handing over an inert process provides no standalone value, undermining why the counterpart would see it as a beneficial cooperative move.

residue.item: M&M in the rider: one party inserts a trivial, specific instruction to see if the other reads the whole contract, as the "no brown M&Ms" clause; the carrier is an arbitrary compliance check, the first move is safe because the cost is near zero and the return is information on attention, and the residue is an inspection-mindset where the partner is watched for the smallest slip; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: A compliance test embedded inside an already negotiated and signed contract, not an ignition mechanism between strangers without shared history.

residue.item: Joint bid on the board: two parties bid as a single entity for a contract neither could win alone, as two builders bid for a bridge; the carrier is a merged identity, the first move is safe because the win is impossible otherwise, and the residue is a forced marriage for the life of the project where friction is hidden; both hands strike it at once.
residue.why: Submitting a joint bid requires an extensive prior legal agreement (JV), violating the 'no contract' boundary condition.

residue.item: Credit at the yard: one party pays a supplier to hold materials for the other's use, as a developer pays for the steel a fabricator will use; the carrier is a pre-paid external account, the first move is safe because the money is already out of the giver's hands and the receiver gets tangible value, and the residue is a locked-in supply chain; one side strikes it alone.
residue.why: Paying a supplier for materials does not make the move safe for the payer, who risks their upfront capital if the other defaults.

residue.item: Shared drain in the field: two parties dig a ditch that crosses both properties to solve a flood, as two farmers or two homeowners; the carrier is a continuous physical trench, the first move is safe because the work is done in the open and both gain, and the residue is that the water doesn't care about the line and a block on one side floods both; both hands strike it at once.
residue.why: Duplicate mechanism of 'Wall neither can lift' (a shared physical liability solved by a joint trench/drain).

residue.item: Bucket in the fire: the carrier is a catastrophe that spreads if not stopped, the first move is safe because the risk of the flame jumping is higher than the cost of the water, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the bond is purely reactive and dies with the heat.
residue.why: Skips the required initial descriptive clause and illustrative examples, violating the established structure and grain.

residue.item: Roof in the storm: the carrier is a hostile environment that makes being alone fatal, the first move is safe because the stranger adds utility or body heat at no marginal cost to the shelter, nobody strikes it, and the residue is that the cooperation is a function of the barometer and evaporates at the clearing.
residue.why: Fails formatting by omitting the opening definition and concrete examples of the mechanism.

residue.item: Tow for the ditched: the carrier is a physical blockage on a shared path, the first move is safe because the mover risks only a chain while the ditched is already at zero, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the favor is unpriced and the parties return to their separate miles.
residue.why: Violates the list's strict grammatical structure by skipping directly to 'the carrier is...'.

residue.item: Bracing the beam: the carrier is an immediate structural failure, the first move is safe because the alternative is being crushed, both hands at once strike it, and the residue is that the cooperation lasts only as long as the weight and neither party learned how the other works standing.
residue.why: Lacks the required opening description and concrete operator-grade examples present in every existing item.

residue.item: Hotfix for the exploit: the carrier is a critical failure in a live system, the first move is safe because the damage of the breach outweighs the risk of the intrusion, one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the observer now knows the vulnerability and the owner can never trust the perimeter.
residue.why: Structurally flawed; skips the opening mechanism definition and illustrative cases.

residue.item: Tandem by order: the carrier is a shared hazard that an authority orders two rivals to mitigate, as a dispatcher sends two tugs to one listing ship or a foreman pulls two crews to one leak; the first move is safe because the order provides the legal cover and the hazard is the priority, a third with a stake strikes it, and the residue is that the cooperation is a command-artifact and the parties return to rivalry once the order is lifted.
residue.why: Fails the structural grain of the list by omitting the initial description of the action.

residue.item: In the stance of control, what must be pinned down in writing is the release: the document that converts a reversible nuisance into a final settlement, since without the paper, the duress has no exit and the residue is a legal bill.
residue.why: Written as a theoretical commentary rather than following the list's rigid item format.

residue.item: Fence across the path: the carrier is a physical obstruction on land the other party uses but does not clearly own, the first move is safe because the barrier can be moved and the only loss is a day’s access, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the informal use is permanently ended and every future crossing is a priced easement; the author infers that the boundary is the only thing the writing actually preserves.
residue.why: Missing the core opening clause defining the mechanism and providing an illustrative example.

residue.item: Cloud on the title: the carrier is a low-cost procedural lien or a copyright strike that freezes a larger transaction, the first move is safe because the claim can be withdrawn for a fee and the underlying value is merely delayed, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the nuisance fee becomes the permanent floor for every future negotiation; not a summoned witness, because the audience is a bureau that cannot judge the truth, only record the block.
residue.why: Fails structural formatting by skipping directly to the carrier definition.

residue.item: Tool in the trunk: the carrier is the temporary possession of a necessary tool the other party left unattended, the first move is safe because the tool is kept in working order and its absence merely pauses the work to force a meeting, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the owner must now buy security and the cooperation is a hostage-negotiation for the duration of the job; not a hostage before the ask, where the giver hands over their own asset, since here the hostage is taken.
residue.why: Omits the required initial description of the action and its concrete examples.

residue.item: Domain on the shelf: the carrier is a positional asset like a URL or a trademark with no value to the holder except as a block to the counterpart, the first move is safe because the holder risks only a registration fee, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the stager is marked as a predator and the cooperation is a one-off ransom that leaves no room for a second turn; adjacent to the lot you can lose, but the lot here is the other’s name.
residue.why: Lacks the opening definition and illustrative examples required by the list's format.

residue.item: Feet under the table: the carrier is a physical or professional presence in a space where the other party’s work happens, as a squatter in a storefront or a freelancer who starts a task unasked, the first move is safe because the mover can be ignored or evicted at a cost higher than a conversation, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is that the relationship is born of exhaustion and the first term is a payoff to leave; not a gift already eaten, because the service is an unrequested friction.
residue.why: Missing the introductory clause that describes the mechanism in action.

residue.item: Sand in the gears: the carrier is a reversible technical bottleneck or a bug introduced by a vendor that only they can fix, the first move is safe because the system is slowed rather than broken and the solution is the first cooperative act, one side alone can strike it, and the residue is a forced dependency where the user pays a recurring fix fee for a problem the partner invented; the author infers that a discovered glitch converts the partner into an enemy, making this the riskiest ignition.
residue.why: Fails the strict structural pattern by omitting the mechanism's definition and example.

residue.item: Grade in the bin: the good is reduced to a standard certificate and commingled with the same class from a thousand strangers, as a farmer dumps grain into an elevator or a refinery accepts crude by specification; the carrier is a third-party inspection that strips the source from the good, the first move is safe because the sample represents the whole and the buyer pays for the class, not the farm, the analytical inference is that a third with a stake strikes it, and the residue is a race to the floor, since any quality above the minimum is given away for free and the pool's average drifts toward the bottom.
residue.why: Explicitly excluded by the boundary claim: parties transact with an institutional standard/elevator and never cooperate with each other directly.

residue.item: Tick in the book: the trade is made with whichever stranger occupies the next slot in a priority list, as a stock trader hits the bid on an exchange or a passenger takes the next cab in the rank; the carrier is a time-price priority rule, the first move is safe because the protocol guarantees the best available terms regardless of who provides them, the analytical inference is that one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the price is the only signal, so the parties cannot negotiate a bulk discount or a loyalty term and the relationship ends at the fill.
residue.why: Fails the boundary claim; parties transact with an exchange algorithm rather than cooperating directly with a stranger.

residue.item: Margin at the center: every party transacts only with a central entity that steps between them and nets their obligations, as a clearinghouse becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer in a futures market; the carrier is a novated contract where the stranger's name is replaced by the house's, the first move is safe because the house's collateral pool absorbs any one stranger's default, the analytical inference is that a third with a stake strikes it, and the residue is a systemic ceiling, where the cooperation is only as safe as the house and a single failure becomes total.
residue.why: Transacting with a central clearinghouse means the parties never cooperate with each other, violating the boundary claim.

residue.item: Score on the sheet: a stranger’s history is condensed into a single index by a party who has seen their other deals, as a lender approves a loan based on a credit score or a landlord accepts a tenant based on a background check; the carrier is an aggregated reputation score, the first move is safe because the score predicts the default rate across a thousand similar strangers, the analytical inference is that one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the parties cooperate with the metric rather than each other, so the behavior that moves the number replaces the behavior the number was meant to measure.
residue.why: Interacting with an aggregated institutional credit score is not a direct cooperative move between two strangers.

residue.item: Swap in the pool: the price is set by the volume of goods already held in a reserve, as a decentralized exchange allows a stranger to swap tokens against a pre-funded asset pool; the carrier is an automated mathematical constant, the first move is safe because the reserve is already present and the protocol cannot refuse the trade at the calculated price, the analytical inference is that one side alone strikes it, and the residue is that the cooperation is priced by its own size, so the larger the deal grows the more it costs to move the needle and the relationship is purely mechanical.
residue.why: A DEX liquidity pool is an automated system where parties never interact or cooperate with each other, explicitly excluded.

residue.item: Blanket for the catalog: a single payment buys the right to use every asset in a category without naming or knowing the owners, as a broadcaster pays a performing rights organization to play any song or a manufacturer pays a patent pool; the carrier is a blanket license, the first move is safe because the pool guarantees indemnity against its members, the analytical inference is that a third with a stake strikes it, and the residue is that the parties never meet, the individual's value is obscured by the average, and the pool becomes a gatekeeper that prices out the small.
residue.why: A blanket license explicitly prevents the parties from ever meeting or cooperating directly, failing the boundary condition.
